ANALYSIS COMPLETE (executed script: analysis_worldbank_education_gdp.py; full log: outputs/analysis_results.txt).

FINAL NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS
Grounded in this dataset — where the income measure is actually GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$) and the education measure is "Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI)", with "developing countries" proxied by the Lower-middle-income (LMC) aggregate — the data do not support a robust positive effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita income in either group, and they provide no reliable evidence that the effect differs between developing countries and Sub-Saharan Africa. In the LMC group (complete 1975–2015 series), the long-run level association is negative (≈ −12% GNI per +1pp of education expenditure, HAC p≈0.04, with enrollment controls) but this is heavily trend-driven (Durbin–Watson ≈ 0.2–0.7, severe serial correlation); the year-over-year (first-differenced) association is small and positive (≈ +2% to +3% per +1pp, HAC p≈0.02–0.035) but flips sign and loses significance once labor-force and export controls or lag structures are added (−2.7%, p=0.59; lagged split ≈ 0, both n.s.; 5-year moving-average FD −13.5%, p=0.14). For Sub-Saharan Africa, the dependent variable exists only for 2011–2015 (5 observations), during which the education share mechanically fell (3.65→3.15) while GNI per capita drifted up (1,555→1,634 US$), producing a spurious strongly negative slope (≈ −10% per +1pp, n=5) that cannot be distinguished from trend. The pooled 2011–2015 interaction model (n=10 group-years) yields SSF −10.0% vs LMC −65.9% per +1pp (interaction p<0.001), but this is a 10-point trend artifact of the overlapping window and is treated as secondary, not as the comparative finding. Bottom-line hypothesis: at this two-aggregate-group level of analysis, education expenditure as a share of GNI shows no stable, sign-consistent relationship with per-capita income over time in either group; any apparent cross-group difference (both point estimates negative, SSA's less negative than LMC's in the pooled window) is dominated by limited overlapping coverage (2011–2015), serial correlation, and group-level trends rather than by a genuine differential effect of education spending.

KEY ESTIMATES (all semi-elasticities: % change in GNI pc per +1pp of education-expenditure share)
- LMC level 1975–2015 + enrollment controls: −12.05% (HAC p=0.040, n=41, DW=0.38)
- LMC level 1991–2015 all controls: −15.36% (HAC p=0.170, n=25)
- LMC FD bivariate: +2.19% (HAC p=0.035, n=40) | FD + enrollment controls: +2.66% (HAC p=0.017, n=40) | FD all controls: −2.71% (p=0.589, n=24) | FD lag split: ~0 (n.s.)
- LMC 5-yr MA FD: −13.50% (HAC p=0.144, n=32)
- SSF level 2011–2015 bivariate: −10.00% (n=5)
- Pooled interaction 2011–2015: SSF −10.00% vs LMC −65.86% (interaction p<0.001, n=10)
Descriptives: SSF educ-exp decade means 4.37→4.64→4.71→3.62→3.15; LMC 3.52→3.54→3.69→3.31→3.06; corr(educ, ln GNI): SSF −0.967 (over 5 yrs), LMC −0.434 (over 41 yrs).

DIAGNOSTICS ACTUALLY RUN
- Newey–West HAC standard errors (4 lags in level/FD models; 2 lags in the n=10/n=5 overlap models) to address serial correlation.
- First differencing of all variables (contemporaneous, with controls, and with 1-year lag of Δeduc).
- Durbin–Watson on every regression (reported per model; levels show DW 0.2–1.5, confirming trend/serial-correlation contamination of level estimates).
- Sample-size-aware design: asymmetric windows (LMC full 41 years; SSF its actual 5-year GNI window), pooled interaction only on the common window, flagged as secondary per your instruction.

CONSEQUENTIAL ASSUMPTIONS (explicit, as requested)
1. LMC ("Lower middle income") ≈ "developing countries" in the question — a mapping assumption, not verifiable from the file.
2. The outcome analyzed is GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$, NY.GNP.PCAP.KD), not "GDP (2010 US$)" as the dataset description claims; the column description matches the file and the file was treated as ground truth.
3. The education measure is Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI, NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS), not government expenditure on education (% of total expenditure) as the description claims.
4. Missing cells are true blanks (no '..' sentinels); SSF GNI exists only 2011–2015 and SSF exports/labor-force series only 1991–2015 — the heaviest-missingness years are all pre-1991 SSF.
5. Groups are aggregates, not countries: n=2 units means clustered SEs are not credible (2 clusters), so within-group differenced comparisons were promoted to primary evidence and the pooled interaction demoted to secondary, per your guidance. All statements are associational; reverse causality (income → education budgets) cannot be addressed with these variables, and the first-difference estimates should be read as short-run associations, not causal effects.

payload.hypothesis: In these two World Bank aggregates (LMC proxying developing countries; SSF for Sub-Saharan Africa), there is no robust, sign-consistent effect of increasing the education-expenditure share of GNI on per-capita income in either group, and no reliable evidence that the effect differs between them: LMC long-run level associations are negative but trend-driven (DW~0.2-0.4), LMC year-over-year associations are small and positive but fragile (+2 to +3% GNI per +1pp, sign-flipping with controls/lags), and SSA can only be estimated over 2011-2015 (n=5), where a mechanically negative slope (-10% per +1pp) arises because the education share fell while GNI drifted up. The pooled interaction comparison (SSF -10% vs LMC -66% per +1pp, n=10) is a small-sample trend artifact and is treated as secondary. Caveats: GNI (constant 2015 US$) analyzed rather than GDP (2010 US$), education measured as % of GNI rather than % of total expenditure, LMC stands in for 'developing countries', and aggregate two-unit data support associational claims only.
payload.workflow: Wide CSV reshaped to a group-year panel (2 groups x 6 series x 41 years); completeness audited (SSF GNI only 2011-2015, n=5; LMC complete); asymmetric-window estimation per researcher instruction: (1) LMC full-sample OLS with Newey-West HAC SEs, (2) LMC first-differenced regressions (bivariate, enrollment controls, all controls, lagged-educ split, 5-yr MA FD) as primary evidence, (3) SSF bivariate slope on its 2011-2015 GNI window, (4) pooled interaction model on the 2011-2015 overlap (n=10) as secondary; Durbin-Watson diagnostics on every model; effect sizes reported as % change in GNI pc per +1pp education-expenditure share; script analysis_worldbank_education_gdp.py, log outputs/analysis_results.txt.
